title: Mineral‐Associated Carbon Accrual Masks Labile Particulate Carbon Loss in Permafrost Region on the Tibetan Plateau
content:
Unsaturated MAOC pools sustain Tibetan permafrost SOC accumulation. Under high emissions, however, L-POC declines, with the fastest relative loss occurring at intermediate depths (10–30 cm), despite ubiquitous H-POC gains. These depth-dependent fraction dynamics demonstrate that resolving soil layers and fractions is essential to predict permafrost carbon feedbacks.


ABSTRACT

Permafrost regions store vast quantities of soil organic carbon (SOC), yet the future trajectories of functionally distinct SOC fractions across soil depths remain poorly constrained. Integrating depth-explicit soil fractionation data from 104 sites across the Tibetan permafrost region with a process-based SOC model, we project century-scale dynamics of particulate (POC) and mineral-associated organic carbon (MAOC) under three emission scenarios. We show that MAOC currently comprises 56.5% of regional total SOC stock and remains far from saturation throughout the profile. Consistent with this large stabilization capacity, total SOC was projected to increase over the 21st century under all scenarios, with the largest gains under SSP5-8.5. However, this positive net gain masked a significant restructuring of SOC fractions. MAOC accumulated across all depths and scenarios, and heavy POC remained comparatively buffered, whereas light POC declined under SSP5-8.5. The strongest relative light POC losses occurred in the 10–30 cm layers, where warming-driven decomposition remained strong while plant-C input compensation weakened. These divergent trajectories indicate a shift toward a “carbon-rich yet energy-poor” state, where mineral-bound carbon increases while the labile particulate pool supporting microbial activity is depleted. Our findings reveal SOC vulnerability in permafrost region is governed by both fraction identity and soil depth, and that net SOC gains can conceal the loss of metabolically active carbon. Incorporating measurable, depth-resolved SOC fractions into Earth system models is therefore essential for constraining permafrost–climate feedbacks.
